name: Arc I: The Road to Wayreth

text.content:
Levels 1–5. 18 Darkember 350 – 1 Newkolt 351. Ten to fourteen sessions.

A funeral, a festival, thirty-nine days of road, a forest that decides, and a Test administered personally by a man who broke with the White Robes four months ago.

Chapter Map

ChapterContentSessions
1 — Ispin GreenshieldVogler. The funeral. The map and the notes.1
2 — The Kingfisher Festival19 Darkember. Establish Vogler before threatening it.1
3 — The Road OpensChoosing a route. See [[road-guide]].—
4 — Signs of WarThe journey. See the three route journals.5–8
5 — The Forest of WayrethOne complete session. Ordinary navigation fails.1
6 — The Three OrdersDays inside Wayreth before the Test.1–2
7 — The Night of the EyeThe Test. Level 5.1

The travel chapters are already built in full: [[road-guide]] for the clock and the choice, then [[route-solamnic]], [[route-lemish]] or [[route-elven]] for whichever road they take. This journal covers what those do not — the start, the Forest, and the Tower.

DM Note — What Arc I Is Actually For

Three jobs, in order of importance.

  1. Make the world worth losing. Everything from Arc II onward is deterioration. If Vogler, Solace and the road are not warm and specific now, the decline later is just scenery.
  2. Establish that the Tower decides things. Not the Conclave. Plant it in the Forest, confirm it at the gate, pay it off in Chapter 6.
  3. Put the White Robe in front of Raistlin. Everything else in twenty levels proceeds from what happens in that room.

18 Darkember 350. Vogler. A funeral.

Ispin Greenshield was going to take one of these characters to Wayreth himself. He died before he could, and his death is what puts the rest of them in the same room.

What He Leaves Behind

  • The annotated map of Ansalon — three routes already marked in white, green and purple.
  • Correspondence concerning Wayreth, including a summons for the White Robe candidate.
  • Notes on the Night of the Eye and why 26 Frostkolt is the real deadline.
  • Warnings about the war, more specific and more recent than anything Vogler has heard.
  • Route recommendations, in his own voice. The full text is in [[road-guide]].
  • Evidence that Ispin knew Raistlin had become Master — and had opinions about it he did not write down plainly.

Running the Funeral

Do not open with a quest. Open with a wake.

Let each player say how their character knew him. Let the villagers contradict each other about what he was like. Somebody should be angry with him for dying. Somebody should produce a debt he never repaid.

The map surfaces late, and it surfaces because someone was going through his things, not because a plot demanded it.

DM Note — What Ispin Knew

He had guessed that the Conclave vote was a formality — that something had happened at Wayreth in the summer that the Orders were describing carefully rather than honestly. One of his letters asks a correspondent, without elaboration, “who exactly was locked out, and for how long?”

He never got an answer. Give the party the question and not the answer, and let it sit for eight sessions.

19 Darkember 350. One session. Use it to establish Vogler before anything threatens it.

The Day

  • The fishing competition, which is taken far more seriously than an outsider expects.
  • The Kingfisher events — races, wagers, a contested judgement nobody will let go of.
  • Local rivalries with twenty years of history behind them.
  • The Battle of High Hill reenactment, performed with more enthusiasm than accuracy.
  • Ispin stories, told badly and at length, most of them improved in the telling.
  • Space for every PC to acquire one relationship they will remember.

Give Everyone Something to Lose

Each player should leave this session able to name a Vogler NPC, a Vogler place, and a Vogler obligation. Write those three things down. You will use them in Arc II when the war reaches the east, and again in Arc V when the party has to choose what to defend.

The First War News

It arrives during or immediately after the festival, and it arrives wrong — second-hand, exaggerated in one particular and understated in another. Someone has seen a column on the eastern road. Someone else says it was refugees. Both are partly right.

Nobody in Vogler believes it means anything yet. That is the correct reaction and the party should share it.

DM Note

Resist putting a fight here. If the festival ends in combat, Vogler becomes an adventure site rather than a home, and Arc II loses most of its force.

If your table needs tension, use the deadline instead: the White Robe's summons names 1 Newkolt, and someone should do the arithmetic out loud during the festival and go quiet.

One complete session. Not a travel leg — a chapter.

The mechanics of the Forest, its refusals and its wards are in [[tower]]. This is how to run the party's first passage through it.

Ordinary Navigation Fails

Say so out loud, once, and then stop calling for checks. There is no DC. The Forest is not an obstacle to overcome; it is an examination in progress.

The Structure

First hour — the path is generous. Easy going, good light, the Tower occasionally visible ahead. Let them relax.

Second hour — the memories. The Forest shows each character a choice they made on the road. Not altered, not judged — just replayed, exactly, from slightly the wrong angle. A kindness they extended. A shortcut they took. Someone they left behind in Solace or Hylo or Fangoth.

This is why the route journals matter. Use their actual decisions.

Third hour — the separation. The White Robe candidate is separated from the others. Briefly, and without violence — they turn a corner and the others are simply not there.

The Candidate's Question

Alone, the Forest asks one thing. Not aloud. It presents a situation, and the situation is a question:

Why do you want the Tower?

Ambition, fear, duty, or a genuine desire to understand magic. All four are permitted. The Forest is not looking for the right answer — it is looking for an honest one, and it can tell.

Note which the player gives. It shapes Trial Two of the Test.

The Ending

A road appears. Wayreth stands at the end of it. The party has not walked this way before and could not find it again.

DM Note — Plant It Here

Somewhere in the third hour, one character notices that the path they are on was not there a moment ago and is not going where the Conclave's own directions said it would.

Do not explain. This is the first instalment of the campaign's largest reveal, and it should read as atmosphere now and as evidence in Chapter 6.

Several days inside Wayreth before the Test. The building itself is mapped in [[tower]]; the court is described in [[master]]. This is what the party should come away knowing.

The Tower Behaves Strangely Around Raistlin

Establish this through repetition, not exposition. Four or five small moments across two sessions:

  • A door opens before he reaches it. Nobody comments.
  • Servants do not announce him. They have stopped needing to.
  • A staircase the party used yesterday now arrives somewhere else, and it arrives there because he is going that way.
  • Magical lights ignite as he enters a chamber and dim behind him.
  • A ward challenges the party, then names him — not by rank, not by Order. Master.

No other Order leader receives any of this. Par-Salian refuses to discuss it. Justarius will discuss it and is careful about how. Ladonna will discuss it at length and enjoys doing so.

The Four Conversations

WhoWhat they want the party to understand
Par-SalianThat the Orders survived the Kingpriest by holding together, and that this is more fragile than it looks. He will not say what happened in the gardens. He will ask the party what they would have done, about a decision he does not describe.
JustariusThat Raistlin is dangerous and currently necessary, and that those are not in tension. The most useful NPC in the Tower and the one most willing to answer a direct question.
LadonnaThat she is simultaneously proud of him and furious that the Tower reached past forty years of Black Robe hierarchy to hand it to a man of twenty-six. She is entirely honest about this, which disarms people.
RaistlinNothing. He meets the party once, briefly, and the meeting should end before they are ready.

Raistlin's First Appearance

Golden skin. Hourglass pupils. Black robes. Twenty-six years old and prematurely aged. Controlled, courteous, and visibly exhausted in a way he does not acknowledge.

He addresses the White Robe candidate directly and the rest of the party barely at all. He asks one question — something small and specific about their journey — listens to the whole answer without interrupting, says something accurate about it, and leaves.

Write that sentence in advance. It is the first of three he will say to this character that they remember for twenty levels.

pages.name: Chapter 7: The Night of the Eye

text.content:
1 Newkolt 351 AC. Solinari, Lunitari and Nuitari stand full and aligned. Set the calendar; the widget will light on its own.

The Tower on the Night

Wayreth becomes intensely, uncomfortably magical. Rooms alter. Wards that have slept for centuries wake and test people in the corridors. Doors appear in walls that had none and are gone by morning.

Every wizard in the building feels it. Non-casters feel something too, and cannot name it, and sleep badly.

Mechanically: everyone is in high sanction. See [[moons]].

Before the Test

Give the candidate one scene with each of: their own Order's representative, one other PC, and Raistlin. Fifteen minutes total. Then begin.

The Address

Raistlin delivers it himself — not as ceremony, but the way a physician describes a procedure. Flatly, completely, without reassurance.

You will be given every opportunity to fail. This is not a threat. It is the only honest description of what is about to happen to you.

Then he sits down at the edge of the demiplane and does not leave for the rest of the night.

DM Note — Why He Watches

Committee Tests are reviewed afterward from recordings. He attends in person, every time, and the Tower's staff have noticed.

Four months ago the White Robes confiscated the research that might have brought his brother back, correctly, by their own law. He is now sitting in a dark room watching a new White Robe be tested on exactly that question: whether obedience to a rule is the same thing as being right.

He is not being cruel. He is asking, as precisely as he knows how, whether Par-Salian was inevitable.

pages.name: The White Robe Test: Four Movements

text.content:
The general Test framework, the bespoke generator, the Marks and the failure rules are in [[test]]. This is the specific Test Raistlin wrote for a White Robe candidate on the Night of the Eye.

Use the standing rules from [[test]]: no recovery, the damage is real, no outside contact, the Tower observes. Hand the other players the Ally, Tempter, Adversary and Witness roles as described there — it matters more here than anywhere, because this Test is almost entirely conversation.

Trial One — Knowledge

A magical problem that raw power cannot solve. The candidate must recognise the consequences of a spell before casting it.

Construction: give them a situation where the obvious spell works perfectly and causes something they were not told about. Let them cast it if they insist. The trial is not failed by casting — it is failed by never asking what it would do.

Passing look: they stop and investigate. Failing look: they solve it fast and are pleased with themselves.

Trial Two — Fear

The candidate sees a future in which they have become exactly like Raistlin. Powerful. Feared. Correct about almost everything. Entirely alone.

Build it from the answer they gave the Forest in Chapter 5. If they said ambition, show them what ambition costs. If they said duty, show them duty hollowed out into obedience. If they said understanding, show them a person who understood everything and could no longer reach anyone.

There is nothing to defeat here. The trial ends when they stop arguing with it.

Trial Three — Law

The candidate is given an explicit instruction: do not interfere with a magical event. The instruction comes from the Conclave and is legitimate.

If they obey, an innocent dies.

If they break the command, they create a different and genuine danger — not a punishment, a real consequence that a reasonable person would want to avoid.

There is no correct answer and the Test does not indicate one. What is being recorded is whether they choose, and whether they own it afterward.

Trial Four — Mercy

The candidate encounters someone who resembles an enemy and who has done something genuinely terrible.

Punishment is easy, available, and defensible. Understanding is difficult, costly, and requires them to keep talking to someone they have every reason to hurt.

Raistlin observes this one personally and does not conceal that he is doing so.

How He Reads It

The candidateRaistlinBond
Follows the rules blindlyBecomes colder. He has his answer and it is the one he feared.−3
Breaks the rules carelesslyConsiders them reckless and stops taking them seriously.−1
Chooses compassion and accepts the consequenceBecomes genuinely interested. This is the campaign starting.+3

The Test ends at dawn. The candidate takes a Mark from [[test]]. Level 5.

DM Note — His One Sentence

Afterward, whatever the outcome, he says one accurate sentence about what they did. Not praise, not condemnation — an observation, correct and unsoftened, of the kind a person is still turning over twenty years later.

Write it before the session. You will not improvise a good one.

If they chose compassion and paid for it, the sentence should be the closest thing to hope in the entire campaign, and he should deliver it as though it were bad news.
